title: Six years
hook: years of hard austerity; some think he has died

segments.voice: Yesterday, dukkarakarika: the wanderer starved until his spine showed like a string of beads. Starving isn't holy.

Brave, or just stubborn? From inside a long, hard stretch, a degree that takes years, a job that can't be left, caring for someone who is ill, the two can look exactly the same. So can pushing on and being stuck. Tradition says the wanderer spent six years this way, in the forests near Uruvela. Breathless meditation. Fasting. Standing instead of sitting. Lying on a bed of thorns, by his own later account. His five companions watching, waiting. And in the later telling, one day he collapses.
screen: `BRAVE, OR JUST STUBBORN?` → `SIX YEARS IN THE FOREST.` → `ONE DAY HE COLLAPSES.`

segments.voice: In the Buddha's own account, there's a strange moment. When some gods saw him, they said, the wanderer Gotama is dead. Others said, he's not dead, but he's dying. Others said, he's neither: this is simply how an awakened one lives. Nobody could tell. The later telling makes it vivid. He faints while walking and falls to the ground, and a god runs to his father, King Suddhodana: your son is dead. The old king, who had tried so hard to keep him in the palace, refuses to believe it. My son will not die, he says, before he reaches what he went looking for. Six years. The Buddha's own account gives no number; the six years come from later tradition. But the length is the point. This wasn't a weekend. It was years of a life, given completely to one method. And the Buddha's verdict, looking back, is calm and devastating. Whatever painful feelings any ascetic has ever felt, past, present or future, this was the utmost. There's none beyond it. And still, it didn't lead to awakening. The Buddha isn't against effort. He'll later make right effort part of the path. But effort pointed the wrong way only digs deeper into the wrong place. A shovel works hard in a hole, too.
screen: `DEAD, DYING, OR AWAKE?` · `MY SON WILL NOT DIE YET.` · `NO ASCETIC HAD FELT MORE PAIN.` · `EFFORT POINTED THE WRONG WAY.` · then, large: `HARDER ISN'T ALWAYS BETTER.`

segments.voice: Sit, or lie down if you can, notice where you're tired, the eyes, the back, the legs, the mind, and admit it gently to yourself: I'm tired here. Don't fix it or push through it; on each out-breath, let that place get a little heavier, a little more supported by the chair or the floor. You're allowed to rest; the Buddha found out the hard way.
Six years. The time tradition gives to the wanderer's austerities: pain, he says, no ascetic had gone beyond, and still not the way.
Your line: harder isn't always better. Even the hard way has an end. Day forty-six, done.

howItsDone: Buddhists speak of the six years of austerities as the extreme the Buddha tried and set aside, and teachers use them to warn against self-punishment in practice as well as against laziness.

original.note: Pali (Sanskrit tapas): heat, austerity, the burning practice of self-denial the ascetics believed would purify.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha meditated in the forest for six years.
what it means: he spent years in extreme self-denial, and found that harder isn't always better.
what a scholar hears: MN 36 has deities disagree whether he is dead, dying or an arahant; the six-year figure and Suddhodana's refusal come from the Nidanakatha.

a jolt of urgency from seeing life plainly

chat.says: So did all those years of hard practice finally pay off?
options: No. He said no ascetic felt more pain, yet it didn't bring awakening.
Yes. The pain finally broke through, and that's how he awakened.
No, because he gave up after only a few weeks of it.
chat.meaning: His verdict: no ascetic had felt pain beyond his, and still it didn't lead to awakening. Effort pointed the wrong way digs deeper.

Uruvela.meaning: the forest place where he did his austerities

ascetic.meaning: someone who gives up comforts for a spiritual goal

sources.ref: Mahasaccaka Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 36): the gods' views and the verdict on austerities
Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the six years, the fainting, and King Suddhodana
Mahasihanada Sutta (Majjhima Nikaya 12): the ascetic practices he tried, including standing and a bed of thorns

notes: The six years: traditional (commentaries); MN 36 and MN 26 don't give the number. Confirm.
Lying on thorns: MN 12 lists such practices among those the Bodhisatta tried; the script says 'some tellings say'. Confirm.
MN 36 verdict paraphrased: whatever painful feelings ascetics in past, future or present have felt, this is the utmost. Confirm.
Suddhodana's refusal is paraphrased from the Nidanakatha; confirm.
